title: Statement and Prediction (Assumption, Conclusion, Course of Action, Inference)
shortDescription: Evaluate statements: implicit assumptions, valid conclusions, sensible actions and predictions.
genZNote: These are not opinion questions — only what the statement forces counts. Extreme words (all, only, never) are usually the trap.

sections.heading: Question Types
sections.body: Example: Statement — "Please use the stairs; the lift is under maintenance." Assumption I: The lift cannot be used now — implicit, valid. Assumption II: Everyone prefers stairs — not implied.

table.caption: Types and rules
rows: Implicit, unstated supposition that must hold for the statement to make sense
Follows definitely from the statement; no outside knowledge
Practical, relevant, solves/mitigates the problem; not extreme
Strong = relevant, specific, universal-impact; weak = trivial, emotional, irrelevant
Likely outcome supported by the statement and common sense; avoid certainty claims

sections.heading: Strategy
bullets: Take the statement as true; ignore real-world facts unless asked.
"Definitely true/false", "probably true/false" options: choose probabilistic wording when the statement allows but does not force.
Extreme words (all, only, never, always) usually make an option wrong.
For course of action, prefer measured steps (investigate, review, fix) over drastic ones.
For arguments, check whether the reason is directly relevant to the proposal.

sections.heading: Prediction Reasoning
sections.body: Predictions rest on trends or conditions in the statement: "Rain is forecast; roads are waterlogged" → delays likely. Avoid answers needing facts not stated.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Statement-based reasoning evaluates what is implicit, what follows, what action is sensible and what outcome is likely from a given statement.
keyFacts: Assumption is implicit; conclusion must follow.
Course of action must be practical and relevant.

sources.name: Standard competitive-exam reasoning reference (R.S. Aggarwal, Verbal & Non-Verbal Reasoning)

options: An implicit supposition underlying the statement

questions.prompt: Which words usually signal a weak option?
A good course of action is:
questions.explanation: It should solve or mitigate the problem.
